Here's my defense of the golden parachute bullshit. I don't think this guy deserves $60M, but these are some of the conditions leading to the golden parachute / excessive compensation issue, and some examples of CEOs that deserve it, and others that didn't but got millions anyway.

Basically I think it comes down to the fact that a CEO can have a huge (positive or negative) impact on a company and all companies are competing for a small pool of who they think are qualified for the role. And knowing what we know about hiring practices, they're basically making educated guesses about who the best fit is for the role. Sometimes they get it right and do well, other times they get it horribly wrong. Unfortunately compensation is going to be decided at the outset, and even tying compensation to stock price doesn't entirely fix the problem.

Some points of assumption:

1.) The value of labor is decreasing due to automation

Because of this businesses want cheap labor, not good labor. They can train any monkey to do the job, so they don't want to pay more for someone that can do more, because that's unnecessary. Because of this all the blue collar jobs at a company are facing decreasing salaries in real dollars.

2.) The value of middle managers is going away with AI.

Look at how an amazon warehouse or WMS can help manage workers. Instead of a manager making $80-100k / year reviewing reports and determining who's productive or not and who should stay or go, you can have a heartless algorithm ping workers when they need to work harder and send HR a notice to fire workers that remain below an arbitrary productivity threshold. I don't generally agree with this approach for a number of reasons, but it's happening.

3.) CEOs or leaders of an organization can have a massive impact, either positive or negative. There's no system of "court martial and execution" for incompetent CEOs like the militaries of the past used, but there is a need to recruit the highest potential managers for the CEO job because of its importance. Because of this you have a skewed risk vs rewards ratio. There is a (perceived) low amount of potential CEOs out there and everyone is fighting over them, so that leads to this situation competition over compensation packages and resulting large salaries. Some countries have instituted caps on CEO compensation, but in a world economy wouldn't your best leaders then just go work overseas for 10 times as much?

4.) The Peter Principle, where someone does very well their whole career and then gets promoted one level too high for their ability and proceeds to fail. The important part of this is that they legitimately may have been a superstar employee for 30+ years, and because of this it's hard for some boards of directors to fire them if they're looking too much into past performance. This is why promotions should be based on future potential, and past performance is only an element in that.
